findings.title: Overly permissive verdict regex accepts malformed markdown
findings.why: The loosened regex `[*:\s]*` accepts arbitrary whitespace/asterisk combinations between 'Verdict' and the value, including degenerate cases like `Verdict   *   * PASS` or `Verdict*** ***PASS`. The comment claims to accept 3 orderings but the character class is unbounded. This weakens gate validation and may accept output that doesn't conform to expected markdown conventions.
findings.recommendation: Replace with explicit alternation: `r"(?:^|\n)\s*\*{0,2}[Vv]erdict\*{0,2}\s*:\s*(PASS|FAIL)"` to match only well-formed patterns. Add regression test cases for the degenerate cases that should be rejected.

findings.title: Assembly step glob searches unbounded directory tree
findings.why: The assembly content resolution globs `*.md` over `task_dir.parent` (the project root), potentially scanning thousands of unrelated markdown files in a large repository. Unlike the build-task-file special-case which deliberately excludes parent search (executor.py:283-286), this branch has no scoping justification. Codebase audit findings (agent-A-orchestration.md F-A-11) flag cross-PRD contamination risk.
findings.recommendation: Scope the glob to `task_dir / "results"` and `task_dir` only; remove `task_dir.parent` from search_dirs unless evidence shows subprocess writes to parent. Add early-exit after finding first valid candidate to avoid exhaustive search.

findings.title: Triple-fallback prompt builder swallows TypeError without logging
findings.why: The triple-try convention silently swallows TypeError exceptions with no diagnostic output. When a prompt builder has a genuine signature bug (wrong parameter name, missing required arg), the fallback cascade masks the error and produces a generic string. This makes debugging prompt builder issues difficult and violates the principle of making errors visible.
findings.recommendation: Log each TypeError at debug level with builder_name and attempted signature. Consider using `inspect.signature()` to probe compatibility before attempting each call, failing fast on unexpected signature mismatches.

findings.title: Duplicate agent-block parsing logic across three dual-mode builders
findings.evidence:
def _parse_agent_block(notes: str, agent_idx: int) -> dict:
    import re
    header_pat = re.compile(...)
    # 25 lines of regex extraction logic
findings.why: The `_parse_agent_block` helper is called from `build_investigation_prompt`, `build_web_research_prompt`, and `build_synthesis_prompt` with identical semantics (read research-notes.md, extract Agent N block via regex). The regex compilation happens on every call (no caching). Each dual-mode wrapper has nearly identical config-probing logic (lines 584-614, 703-734, 764-794). This is classic copy-paste duplication violating DRY.
findings.recommendation: Hoist `_parse_agent_block` compilation into module scope with `re.compile()` cached at import time. Extract common config-probing pattern into a shared `_dual_mode_dispatch` decorator that handles *args/**kwargs detection and config.task_dir probing, reducing each builder to a single render call.

findings.title: Dual-mode prompt builders lack test coverage for new executor calling convention
findings.why: The dual-mode wrappers for `build_investigation_prompt`, `build_web_research_prompt`, and `build_synthesis_prompt` add a new calling convention (config + step_id) to support the executor's `_build_prompt(builder_name, step_id=step_id)` call. Existing tests (test_prompts.py:123-138) only verify the legacy positional-args convention. The new branch (step_id extraction, Agent N block parsing, slug generation, mkdir) is untested. Resume logic and assembly content resolution are also untested.
findings.recommendation: Add test cases in `tests/cli/prd/test_prompts.py` covering: (1) dual-mode builders called with (config, context_summaries=None, step_id="investigation-3"), (2) Agent N block extraction from realistic research-notes.md, (3) fallback behavior when research-notes.md is missing or Agent N block is absent, (4) slug generation edge cases (unicode, long titles). Add integration test for assembly glob logic in test_resolve_step_content.py.

findings.title: Resume skip logic in Stage A and Stage B has minimal test coverage
findings.why: The new resume logic (Stage A skip-until index calculation, Stage B substage skip with artifact existence checks) is central to the PR's greenfield-unblocking goal. Test coverage exists for resume_from config propagation (test_e2e.py:364-423) but not for: (1) skip-until boundary conditions (resume_from as first/last Stage A step, Stage B target skipping all of Stage A), (2) artifact-based skip predicates (_should_run + have_investigation/have_web/have_synthesis), (3) context_summaries recording skipped steps.
findings.recommendation: Add unit tests in test_executor.py covering: resume_from="parse-request" (skip index 1), resume_from="investigation" (skip all Stage A), resume_from="synthesis-qa" (skip investigation+web), artifact existence short-circuits (touch research/01-foo.md, assert investigation skipped). Add assertion that skipped steps write to _context_summaries.

findings.title: No path validation on files read by dual-mode prompt builders
findings.why: The dual-mode builders read `config.task_dir / "research-notes.md"` and `config.task_dir / "scope-discovery-raw.md"` without path validation. While `config.task_dir` is derived from user-controlled `--output` (commands.py:48), there's no check that the resolved paths stay within expected boundaries. A malicious or malformed config could point task_dir outside the workspace. The `is_file()` check prevents directory-as-file attacks but not symlink traversal or out-of-tree reads.
findings.recommendation: Add `task_dir.resolve().is_relative_to(expected_root)` validation in config.py after deriving task_dir. Document security assumption that config paths are trusted (CLI-constructed, not user-deserialized). Low severity because the attack surface is CLI args (attacker already has arbitrary code exec), not deserialized config.

findings.title: Unbounded file content read in assembly detection heuristic
findings.evidence:
content = match.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
...
looks_like_prd = (
    "prd" in match.name.lower()
    or "# " in content[:200]
)
findings.why: The assembly branch reads entire file content (`read_text()` with no size limit) for every `*.md` match, then only inspects `content[:200]` for the heuristic. In a repo with large documentation files (10MB+ API references), this wastes I/O and memory. The heuristic check doesn't need the full content.
findings.recommendation: Replace with: `with match.open('r', encoding='utf-8') as f: header = f.read(200)` and check `"# " in header`. Only read full content after heuristic passes and file is selected as best candidate. This mirrors the `_read_file(max_bytes=50_000)` pattern used elsewhere in prompts.py.

findings.title: Commands.py adds resume options without updating docstring examples
findings.evidence:
def resume(
    step_id: str,
    product: str | None,
    output: str | None,
    tier: str,
    ...
) -> None:
    """Resume the PRD pipeline from a halted step.
findings.why: The `resume` command now accepts --product, --output, and --tier options (lines 9-26 in diff) to match the original run's config, but the command docstring (line 172 onwards, not shown in diff view_range but implied) likely doesn't document these new parameters or show updated usage examples. The prd_group docstring (commands.py:27) shows `superclaude prd resume parse-request` without the new options.
findings.recommendation: Update the `resume` command docstring to document the three new options and explain the "must match original run" requirement. Add example: `superclaude prd resume investigation-3 --product my-app --tier standard`. Update prd_group docstring example if it shows resume usage.

cross_cutting_observations.title: Dual-mode *args/**kwargs pattern erases type safety at call sites
cross_cutting_observations.why: The three dual-mode prompt builders (`build_investigation_prompt`, `build_web_research_prompt`, `build_synthesis_prompt`) use `*args, **kwargs` signatures with runtime type probing (`if config is not None and hasattr(config, "task_dir")`). This sacrifices static type checking: mypy/pyright cannot verify call-site compatibility, IDEs lose autocomplete, and refactoring tools can't track parameter renames. The pattern is justified by backward-compatibility with legacy positional-args callers (e.g., external scripts or tests), but no deprecation timeline is documented. The `# type: ignore[no-redef]` suppression (lines 572, 692, 753) silences legitimate redefinition warnings. This is a form of speculative generality anti-pattern — supporting two calling conventions with no clear migration path.
cross_cutting_observations.recommendation: Introduce a deprecation cycle: (1) Add `@deprecated('Use config-based signature')` decorator to legacy callers, (2) Emit DeprecationWarning on positional-args detection, (3) Schedule removal for v5.0. Alternatively, split into `_build_investigation_prompt_legacy()` and `build_investigation_prompt(config, ...)` with the latter calling the former for a grace period, preserving type safety on the new path.

cross_cutting_observations.title: Incremental feature-gating creates implicit dependencies between resume logic and artifact naming
cross_cutting_observations.why: The Stage B resume logic (executor.py:732-740) uses artifact-existence checks (`p.name[:2].isdigit()` for investigation, `web-*.md` for web research, `synth-*.md` for synthesis) that rely on filename conventions established in prompts.py (lines 600, 720, 780). These conventions are not documented as contracts. If a prompt builder changes output_path format (e.g., zero-padding from `{i:02d}` to `{i:03d}`, or renaming `web-` prefix to `external-`), the resume logic silently breaks — steps that should skip will re-run. There's no schema or constant linking the two modules.
cross_cutting_observations.recommendation: Extract artifact-pattern constants into models.py: `INVESTIGATION_PATTERN = r"^\d{2}-.+\.md$"`, `WEB_RESEARCH_PATTERN = r"^web-\d{2}-.+\.md$"`. Use these in both prompts.py (assert output_path matches) and executor.py (artifact detection). Add integration test that verifies resume skip behavior after manually touching artifacts.

cross_cutting_observations.title: Assembly and task-file preserve-guards embed multi-line strings in f-string blocks
cross_cutting_observations.why: The preserve-guard notes in `build_task_file_prompt` (lines 334-360) and `build_assembly_prompt` (lines 1109-1140) embed 15+ line conditional instructions inside f-string interpolation blocks. This harms readability: the prompt template becomes a mix of static instruction text and dynamic conditional blocks, making it hard to see the actual prompt structure. The pattern also duplicates the conditional rendering logic (`if existing_lines >= 400: existing_note = ...`) rather than using a helper function.
cross_cutting_observations.recommendation: Extract preserve-guard logic into helper functions: `_build_task_preserve_note(existing_task_file) -> str` and `_build_assembly_preserve_note(results_dir) -> str`. Return empty string when no guard needed, the full note otherwise. Insert result into prompt template via `{preserve_note}` placeholder. This follows the existing `_read_file()` helper pattern.

notes_for_orchestrator: High-confidence findings focus on: (1) overly permissive regex weakening gate validation, (2) unbounded parent-directory glob creating performance/correctness risk, (3) missing test coverage for new dual-mode calling conventions and resume skip logic. Medium-confidence findings cover architectural concerns (type erasure from *args/**kwargs, tight coupling between resume logic and filename conventions) and error-handling gaps (swallowed TypeErrors). Low-confidence/nit findings address code style (f-string embedding, missing docstring updates). No hardcoded secrets, injection sinks, or critical data-integrity issues found. The dual-mode pattern is sound for backward compatibility but should have a deprecation timeline.
